name: Warzone
label: Revelation
lede: A drummer Agnostic Front let go picked up the mic, turned a Lower East Side squat crew into a band, and gave Revelation Records its catalog number one.

eras.title: From Rat Poison to the front of the stage
eras.text: Raymond "Raybeez" Barbieri, a Washington Heights kid and Navy veteran, was living in Lower East Side squats with Roger Miret and drumming on the first Agnostic Front record. The band he started on the side, first called Rat Poison, became his whole life once he stepped out from behind the kit.

years.h: Raybeez drums on Agnostic Front's United Blood
years.p: Raymond "Raybeez" Barbieri is the drummer on [[Agnostic Front|40b8a690-94e4-4c82-ad0f-73f4b841e46a]]'s debut EP, United Blood. The same year he starts a Lower East Side band called Rat Poison, soon renamed Warzone.
years.xp:
Raybeez met Roger Miret at a [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]] show at Irving Plaza. The two became close friends and lived together in Lower East Side squats, including Apt. X and C-Squat.

Before Warzone settled, Raybeez also played in the short-lived Skinhead Youth with [[Todd Youth|5a277693-a8b6-4d34-b821-4d6b33a08f03]] on bass, Big Al (later of [[Cause for Alarm|1940001f-3270-4d87-9501-eb243d5f9f50]]) on guitar and Billy Psycho on drums.

years.h: Raybeez leaves the drums and becomes Warzone's singer
years.p: About two years in, Raybeez moves from drums to vocals in Warzone. According to No Echo, Roger Miret told him to sing because he was a terrible drummer.
years.xp:
Bandcamp Daily puts it more bluntly: Raybeez made Warzone his main priority after being kicked out of Agnostic Front for being too unstable.

From then on he was the one constant in Warzone. Guitarists, bassists and drummers rotated through for fourteen years, including Todd Youth, [[Walter Schreifels|9f350578-acdd-480e-8273-5eaf88842f1c]] and Roger Miret himself on bass.

eras.title: Revelation's number one
eras.text: By 1986 Warzone had a crew around them, including the Warzone Women, and a sound that Vice credits with leading NYHC's second, bigger wave. Then two kids starting a label heard the band might split and decided the moment had to be pressed onto vinyl.

years.h: As One demo, with the Warzone Women singing along
years.p: Warzone's As One demo comes out as a Some Records tape. Warzone Women CindiB and Bethany sing backing vocals on the song As One at Don Fury's studio.
years.xp:
The Warzone Women formed in late 1985 or early 1986: twenty to thirty women from the scene who flyered, sold shirts, followed the band to Albany and cleared pits by locking hands and spinning. Vice called them non-groupie groupies.

Two of them, Alexa Poli and Gwyn McAllister, put out a joke fanzine around 1986 called Lifestyles of the Poor & Homeless.

yt: Morning Show: NYHC 1986 with Raybeez and Todd Youth
years.h: Raybeez and Todd Youth explain NYHC on morning TV
years.p: A 1986 television morning show segment on New York hardcore features Raybeez and guitarist [[Todd Youth|5a277693-a8b6-4d34-b821-4d6b33a08f03]]. Todd Youth leaves Warzone around 1986 for [[Murphy's Law|4a9fae02-7de0-4cb8-97d7-1fd790d9675e]].

years.h: Pool party gig in Rockland County ends in arrests
years.p: Warzone and Nausea play a pool party at Warzone Woman Brooke Smith's family home in Rockland County. Kids mosh in the pool, and Roger Miret and English Nick are arrested that day.

years.src: Revelation Records pressing history · The Hundreds
years.h: Lower East Side Crew 7" · Revelation No. 1
years.p: Jordan Cooper and [[Ray Cappo|e8357f9d-f7f5-4858-a766-aef004bb38a6]] heard Warzone were talking about breaking up and wanted the band documented. The 7" becomes Revelation's first release, and it sells well enough to keep the label going.
years.xp:
The first pressing was 1,000 black copies with light blue labels hand-drawn in black ink, some B-sides numbered 1 to 100. Forty-one came with white paper labels and a Warzone logo colored in with orange marker.

The 7" went through four pressings by 1989. Six orange copies of the second press came in an alternate sleeve of a lion attacking a horse, and 150 of the 300 clear fourth-press copies went to the band with no sleeves at all.

years.h: Lower East Side Crew release show at CBGB
years.p: Warzone celebrate their Revelation 7" at CBGB. One of the Warzone Women remembered the sound as awful, and the band tearing the place up anyway.

years.h: Warzone live on WNYU
years.p: Warzone play a live session on WNYU's college radio airwaves in New York, later released as Live on WNYU.

years.h: Warzone record their first album at Studio X in New Jersey
years.p: Raybeez, guitarists Paul and Jay Vento, bassist John "Omen" and drummer Lukie Luke cut Don't Forget the Struggle, Don't Forget the Streets at Studio X in Ridgewood, New Jersey, with producer Fink.

eras.title: The cross on the cover
eras.text: Warzone's first album made the title track an NYHC anthem and put a symbol on the cover that people argued about. The next two records moved toward hard rock, and the momentum of 1987 slipped away.

q: Hardcore music is a movement, not a business.
years.h: Don't Forget the Struggle, Don't Forget the Streets
years.p: About 25 minutes of Warzone, out first on the band's own Fist Records, then picked up by Caroline. It opens with a studio skit: Raybeez is missing because he went to get the Warzone Women.
years.xp: The liner notes carried a line that summed up the band's attitude.
play: Don't Forget the Struggle, Don't Forget the Streets
Don't Forget the Struggle, Don't Forget the Streets

years.h: Warzone's album cover gets read as an iron cross
years.p: The cover of Don't Forget the Struggle looked to some like an iron cross, a touchy symbol for a skinhead band. Raybeez answered that American hardcore skinheads stood for patriotism and unity, not racism.
years.xp: Warzone's Lower East Side crowd was mixed, and the band made clear that racist skins weren't welcome. The Warzone Women described Raybeez's whole message as unity across race, gender and money.

years.h: Open Your Eyes, Warzone's second album
years.p: Warzone follow up on Caroline with Open Your Eyes. In 1994 Another Planet pairs it with Don't Forget the Struggle on one reissue.

years.h: Live at the Ritz, NYC, 1988
Warzone's self-titled album goes hard rock
years.p: The self-titled Warzone LP steers toward hard rock. No Echo calls the new direction unsuccessful.

eras.title: The Victory years
eras.text: Raybeez rebuilt Warzone in the '90s on Victory Records, with Don Fury, Bad Brains' Dr. Know and label boss Tony Brummel behind the board. The run ended in September 1997, when he died at 35.

years.h: Live at CBGBs brings Warzone back
years.p: Warzone's first release in four years is a live EP recorded at CBGB, the club where they'd celebrated their first 7".

years.h: Old School to New School, Warzone on Victory
years.p: A covers album produced by [[Don Fury|0bec484f-b890-4823-af64-0e48530f6f6f]], the engineer behind a generation of NYHC records. It starts Warzone's stretch on Victory Records.

years.h: Raybeez gives what becomes Warzone's final interview
years.p: Raybeez talks to Mike of the Droid Rage webzine. The interview isn't published until May 2016, twenty years later.

years.h: Bad Brains' Dr. Know produces The Sound of Revolution
years.p: [[Bad Brains|e919b253-da5b-4aae-a444-6a368376a2d6]] guitarist Dr. Know produces Warzone's The Sound of Revolution for Victory.

years.h: Fight for Justice, produced by Victory's Tony Brummel
years.p: Victory Records founder Tony Brummel produces Fight for Justice, the last Warzone album released in Raybeez's lifetime.

years.h: Raybeez dies at 35, and Warzone ends with him
years.p: Raymond "Raybeez" Barbieri dies of complications from pneumonia at 35, while being treated at a Veterans Health Administration facility. According to Wikipedia, the illness damaged his liver.
years.xp:
An "R.I.P Ray" sign went up at CBGB. Victory Records dedicated its releases to him for more than a year, and benefit shows raised money for the youth causes he supported.

Those causes were part of the band: Raybeez spoke up for drug-free living and for runaway and abused kids, and he was the only member who was in Warzone from start to finish.

eras.title: Tompkins Square remembers
eras.text: Warzone never continued without Raybeez. Victory gathered the '90s records, Revelation brought the first album back, and twenty years after his death the Lower East Side threw him a free show in the park.

years.h: The Victory Years collects Warzone's '90s records
years.p: Victory Records rounds up Warzone's later work on one partial discography.

years.h: Revelation reissues Don't Forget the Struggle as REV 163
years.p: Revelation puts Warzone's first album back out with its original artwork, 29 years after the band's 7" launched the label.

years.h: Raybeez tribute show in Tompkins Square Park
years.p: [[Murphy's Law|4a9fae02-7de0-4cb8-97d7-1fd790d9675e]], Agnostic Front, [[Gorilla Biscuits|0320a32e-b781-40df-bf48-5cb5ee842762]] and [[Madball|c9e0a0f5-9f53-4247-a52d-a3f29d975e17]] play Tompkins Square Park in memory of Raybeez, twenty years after his death.

years.h: Ex-Warzone guitarist Todd Youth dies at 47
years.p: [[Todd Youth|5a277693-a8b6-4d34-b821-4d6b33a08f03]], who left Warzone around 1986 and went on to Murphy's Law, D Generation and [[Danzig|8925a01a-8608-411d-a90b-f3a52d061208]], dies at 47. Wikipedia gives no cause.
